text: Sure. I'm a final year computer science student at Bennett University. Over the last year I interned and worked on a micro frontend dashboard, mostly TypeScript and React, and I built a side project called Relay that lets me control my laptop from my phone. I'm looking for a backend or full stack role where I can work on real systems.
Nice, that’s a good mix of frontend and some systems work. Tell me more about Relay — what problem were you solving, and what’s happening under the hood when you control your laptop from your phone?

I kept walking away from my laptop in the middle of long builds and wanted to trigger things from my phone. There's a small desktop agent and a phone app, and both connect out to a relay server I wrote. They authenticate over HTTP and then upgrade to a WebSocket, so the server just pushes commands to the agent as they arrive.
Makes sense. Why did you go with a relay server instead of connecting the phone directly to the agent on your local network?

The laptop is behind a home router with NAT, so the phone can't reach it directly unless I set up port forwarding, and that wouldn't work on a college network anyway. With a relay, both sides only make outbound connections, so it works anywhere.
Good — outbound-only connections are the right call there. Let’s get to a coding problem.

Okay, let me read it. So I get the prices for each day, I can do many buy and sell transactions but hold at most one unit. Can I assume the prices are non-negative integers? And can the array be empty or have just one day?

Prices are non-negative, yes. The array can be as short as a single day, and you’d return zero in that case since no transaction is possible. Also, you can’t buy and sell on the same day; you must sell before buying again.

text: The agent would keep the last few hundred command ids it has executed in SQLite, with their results. If a command arrives with an id it already has, it skips execution and just sends the stored result again. The check and the insert would happen in one transaction so a crash in between can't cause a double run.
That’s a clean idempotency story. On the fundamentals side — how does a WebSocket upgrade actually happen over HTTP?

text: The client sends a normal HTTP GET with an Upgrade: websocket header, a Connection: Upgrade header, and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols with a Sec-WebSocket-Accept header, which is the key hashed with a fixed GUID and base64 encoded. After that the same TCP connection carries WebSocket frames instead of HTTP.

text: Because hash based collections like HashMap first use hashCode to pick a bucket and then equals to compare inside it. If two objects are equal but have different hash codes they land in different buckets, so lookups fail and you can get duplicates in a HashSet.

text: An inner join returns only rows that match in both tables. A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with nulls where there's no match, right join is the mirror, and full outer keeps everything from both. I'd use a left join for something like listing all users and their orders, including users who have no orders yet.
Right, that covers them well. Last one — in React, what's the difference between state and props, and when would you lift state up?

text: Props are inputs passed from a parent and are read only in the child, state is data a component owns and can change. When two sibling components need the same data, I lift the state up to their closest common parent and pass it down as props along with callbacks to update it.
